x: Kalibangan in Rajasthan, on the Ghaggar, yielded a ploughed field, fire altars and a terracotta plough. Banawali gave a toy plough, but not the ploughed field and fire altars together.
t: Link each Harappan site with its signature find.

x: Lothal in Gujarat had a brick dockyard and was a port for trade with West Asia. Arikamedu was an Indo-Roman port, and Manda and Ropar were inland sites.
t: Recall which Harappan site had the dockyard.

x: Dholavira in the Rann of Kutch is famous for its reservoirs and water-management system. Mohenjo-daro is known for the Great Bath, not reservoirs.
t: Link each Harappan site with its signature feature.

x: The keyed option B is doubtful: Manda in Jammu is in fact on the Chenab and linked to Himalayan timber. Rakhigarhi as the largest Indian site, Bhagwanpura on the Saraswati excavated by J.P. Joshi, and Ropar on the Sutlej are also true, so no statement is clearly incorrect.
t: Check the river and excavator in each statement.

x: Banawali gave a toy terracotta plough and mother goddess figures, Sinauli 125 burials, Burzahom pit dwellings and Sohgaura a Mauryan copper-plate inscription, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the signature find at each site.

x: The First Buddhist Council met at Rajgir (Rajagriha) in the Saptaparni Cave, under Ajatashatru, soon after the Buddha's death. Vaishali hosted the Second, Pataliputra the Third and Kundalavana the Fourth.
t: Recall the place and patron of each Buddhist Council.

x: The councils met at Rajgir (First, under Ajatashatru), Vaishali (Second, Kalashoka), Pataliputra (Third, Ashoka) and Kundalavana in Kashmir (Fourth, Kanishka), giving B, D, A, C.
t: Arrange the councils by their royal patrons.

x: The Buddha was born at Lumbini, attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, gave his First Sermon at Sarnath and attained Mahaparinirvana at Kushinagar, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the life event at each Buddhist site.

x: All three are correct: Mahavira attained nirvana at Pavapuri, he was born near Vaishali and is linked to its Jain tradition, and Sanchi is famous for its Ashokan Buddhist stupa.
t: Check each place association separately.

x: Both are true: Puhar (Kaveripattinam) at the Kaveri mouth was the Chola port and capital, and Korkai was the chief Pandya port, famous for pearls.
t: Link each Sangam port with its dynasty.

x: Muziris was the Chera port, Tondi and Naura were western-coast ports, and Motupalli was the Kakatiya seaport. The code pairs items in order when List-II repeats, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the dynasty or coast of each port.

x: All four are correct: Khajuraho is Chandela, Konark has the Sun Temple, Thanjavur has the Chola Brihadeeswara Temple, and Mahabalipuram is Pallava.
t: Check each temple site against its dynasty.

x: All three are correct: Akbar built Fatehpur Sikri with the Buland Darwaza and Ibadat Khana, Muhammad bin Tughlaq shifted his capital to Daulatabad (Devagiri), and Firuz Tughlaq took about 1,300 Sanskrit manuscripts from the Jawalamukhi temple library at Nagarkot.
t: Check each place with its ruler.

x: Champaran (1917) was the indigo satyagraha, Kheda (1918) the peasant satyagraha, Ahmedabad (1918) the mill workers' strike and Dandi (1930) the Salt March, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the issue of each Gandhian movement.

x: Both are true: Vallabhbhai Patel led the Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928, and the Chauri Chaura violence of February 1922 made Gandhi withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: All four are correct: Nalanda and Takshashila were ancient centres of learning, Vikramashila was a Buddhist university founded by the Pala king Dharmapala, and Nagarjunakonda was a major Buddhist centre in Andhra.
t: Check each centre's association separately.

x: Harappa lies on the Ravi, Mohenjo-daro on the Indus, Ropar on the Sutlej and Manda on the Chenab, where it served Himalayan timber procurement, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the river of each Harappan site.

x: Arikamedu near Puducherry was an Indo-Roman trading port where Roman pottery, amphorae and other objects have been found. Dhauli has Ashokan edicts and Besnagar the Heliodorus Pillar.
t: Link the place with Roman trade finds.

x: All three are correct: Dhauli and Jaugada in Odisha carry Ashoka's Kalinga rock edicts, and Besnagar (Vidisha) has the Heliodorus (Garuda) Pillar linked to the Bhagavata religion.
t: Check each inscription site separately.

x: Mahabalipuram is Pallava, Pattadakal is Chalukyan, Elephanta has the Shaiva cave temple of Shiva, and Ellora has the Kailasanatha Temple with Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the dynasty or feature of each site.

x: All four are correct: Agra, Delhi (Shahjahanabad under Shah Jahan) and Lahore were Mughal imperial centres, and Akbar built the fort at Allahabad (Prayagraj) as a provincial seat.
t: Check each city's Mughal role.

x: Akbar's tomb is at Sikandra near Agra; Akbar began it and Jahangir completed it. Fatehpur Sikri was his capital, not his burial place.
t: Recall where Akbar is buried.

x: Both are true: Vinoba Bhave started the Bhoodan Movement at Pochampalli in Telangana in 1951, and the Tebhaga Movement of 1946 in Bengal was led by the Kisan Sabha.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: In 1857 Bahadur Shah II led at Delhi, Nana Sahib at Kanpur, Begum Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow and Kunwar Singh at Jagdishpur, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the 1857 leader at each centre.

x: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place at Amritsar on 13 April 1919, when General Dyer fired on a peaceful crowd.
t: Recall the city of the 1919 massacre.

x: All four are correct: Vikramashila was a Buddhist university, Ajanta has Buddhist cave paintings, Amaravati has the Satavahana-era Buddhist stupa, and Nagarjunakonda was a Buddhist centre.
t: Check each Buddhist site separately.

x: Both are true: Amaravati has the great Buddhist stupa of the Satavahana period, and Lepakshi's Veerabhadra Temple is a Vijayanagara monument.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: All three are correct: Warangal was the Kakatiya capital, Kondaveedu was a Reddy kingdom capital, and Penukonda was a Vijayanagara stronghold and later capital.
t: Check each place with its dynasty.

x: The Revolt of 1857 began at Meerut on 10 May 1857, when sepoys rose and marched to Delhi.
t: Recall where the 1857 revolt broke out.

x: Sarnath has Ashoka's Lion Capital, the State Emblem; Motupalli was the Kakatiya port of trade and customs seen by Marco Polo; Hampi was the Vijayanagara capital; Delhi was the Sultanate capital, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the main association of each place.

x: I and II are correct: Jagdishpur is in Bihar, and Khan Bahadur Khan led the 1857 revolt at Bareilly. III is false because Jagdishpur was led by Kunwar Singh.
t: Check each 1857 leader against his centre.

x: Megasthenes was the Seleucid envoy to Chandragupta Maurya's court and wrote the Indica. Fa-Hien came under Chandragupta II and Hiuen-Tsang under Harsha.
t: Link each traveller with his ruler.

x: Fa-Hien came for Buddhist pilgrimage and recorded Buddhist India under Chandragupta II. Relics belong to I-Tsing, Hindu learning to Al-Biruni and Nalanda to Hiuen-Tsang.
t: Link each traveller with his subject.

x: Option C is incorrect: Hindu religion, Puranas, Sanskrit and Yoga were studied by Al-Biruni, not I-Tsing. The other three traveller associations are right.
t: Discriminate I-Tsing from Al-Biruni.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Fa-Hien came during Chandragupta II's reign, but his pilgrimage came from his Buddhist faith, not from the reign he visited.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Hiuen-Tsang studied Mahayana Buddhism at Nalanda because of his faith, not because he visited during Harsha's reign.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: I-Tsing travelled in India in 671–695 CE and studied at Nalanda. The 10th century belongs to Al-Masudi and Harsha's reign to Hiuen-Tsang.
t: Recall the period of each Chinese traveller.

x: Al-Biruni came to India with Mahmud of Ghazni and wrote Kitab-ul-Hind on Indian society and learning.
t: Link each traveller with his ruler.

x: Megasthenes wrote of Brahmins and Shramanas, Fa-Hien of Buddhist pilgrimage, Hiuen-Tsang of Mahayana and Nalanda, and I-Tsing of Buddhist relics and pilgrimage, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Link each traveller with his subject.

x: The Arab traveller Al-Masudi visited India in the 10th century and described the Sun Temple at Multan.
t: Link the traveller with Multan.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Al-Masudi lived in the 10th century, and his account of the Multan Sun Temple does not explain when he lived.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Ibn Battuta, the Moroccan traveller, served Muhammad bin Tughlaq and recorded the Delhi Sultanate in his Rihla.
t: Recall the ruler Ibn Battuta served.

x: I and II are correct: I-Tsing travelled in 671–695 CE and Al-Masudi was a 10th-century visitor. III and IV are false because Ibn Battuta served Muhammad bin Tughlaq and Megasthenes served Chandragupta Maurya.
t: Check each traveller with his period.

x: Two are correct: Megasthenes–Brahmins and Shramanas, and Fa-Hien–Buddhist pilgrimage. Pairs 3 and 4 swap I-Tsing and Al-Biruni: I-Tsing wrote on Buddhist relics and Al-Biruni on Hindu learning.
t: Check each pair, watching for swapped subjects.

x: Ibn Battuta came to Delhi in 1333 and served Muhammad bin Tughlaq as a qazi; his Rihla records the Sultanate.
t: Recall the ruler Ibn Battuta served.

x: I-Tsing's account focuses on Buddhist relics, monastic practice and pilgrimage. Nalanda belongs to Hiuen-Tsang, Hindu learning to Al-Biruni and Multan to Al-Masudi.
t: Link each traveller with his subject.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: I-Tsing landed at Tamralipti, and Hiuen-Tsang's visit to Bodh Gaya concerns another traveller entirely.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Both are true: Hiuen-Tsang visited and described Mathura, and Megasthenes lived at Pataliputra, Chandragupta Maurya's capital.
t: Check each traveller with his place.

x: A is false as keyed: Kushinagar is the classic Hiuen-Tsang stop, though I-Tsing also toured Buddhist holy places, so A is doubtful. B is true: Hiuen-Tsang studied at Nalanda.
t: Discriminate I-Tsing from Hiuen-Tsang.

x: All four are correct: Nicolo Conti (Italian), Abdur Razzaq (Persian), Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz (Portuguese) all visited Vijayanagara.
t: Recall the foreign visitors to Vijayanagara.

x: Megasthenes lived at Pataliputra, Hiuen-Tsang studied at Nalanda, I-Tsing landed at Tamralipti, and Nicolo Conti visited Vijayanagara, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Link each place with its traveller.

x: I, II and III are correct: Megasthenes–Pataliputra, I-Tsing–Tamralipti and Domingo Paes–Vijayanagara. IV is false because Nalanda is linked with Hiuen-Tsang, not Nicolo Conti.
t: Check each traveller with his place.

x: Abdur Razzaq, Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz all visited Vijayanagara, while Hiuen-Tsang visited Bodh Gaya. Only option B pairs Hiuen-Tsang with Bodh Gaya, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-ii, d-iii; the item is untidy because Vijayanagara appears twice yet three travellers need it.
t: Find the one traveller not linked to Vijayanagara.

x: Hiuen-Tsang visited Sarnath, Bodh Gaya, Kushinagar and Mathura, among many places. Megasthenes is linked mainly with Pataliputra, and I-Tsing and Nicolo Conti with none of these.
t: Find the traveller common to several places.

x: Ajatashatru fortified Pataliputra, Harihara and Bukka founded Vijayanagara in 1336, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq built Tughlaqabad, and Ibrahim Adil Shah II founded Nauraspur, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the founder of each city.

x: Both are true: Vijayanagara was founded as a new city on the Tungabhadra in 1336, and its ruins are at modern Hampi in Karnataka.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Harihara I, with his brother Bukka, founded Vijayanagara on the southern bank of the Tungabhadra in 1336. Krishnadeva Raya was a later ruler of the same empire.
t: Recall the founder of Vijayanagara.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Ibrahim Adil Shah II founded Nauraspur, but the musical-city label came from his love of music (Kitab-i-Nauras), not merely from his founding it.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All three are correct: Ajatashatru fortified Pataliputra, his successor Udayin shifted the capital there from Rajagriha, and Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq built Tughlaqabad in Delhi.
t: Check each statement separately.

x: Three were founded as new cities: Vijayanagara, Tughlaqabad and Nauraspur. Pataliputra began as a fortified settlement (Pataligrama) under Ajatashatru. The item is doubtful, since Pataliputra was later a great city.
t: Discriminate a new city from a fort.

x: Krishnadeva Raya founded Nagalapuram near Hampi in honour of his mother, Nagala Devi.
t: Recall the name behind Nagalapuram.

x: Buddha was born at Lumbini, Mahavira at Kundagrama, Adi Shankaracharya at Kaladi in Kerala and Ramanujacharya at Sriperumbudur, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the birthplace of each saint.

x: Basavanna was born at Bagewadi, Kabir at Varanasi, Guru Nanak at Talwandi (Nankana Sahib) and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu at Nabadwip, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
t: Recall the birthplace of each saint.

x: Tulsidas was born at Rajapur, Surdas at Sihi, Mirabai at Kudki and Ramananda at Prayag, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the birthplace of each Bhakti saint.

x: Nizamuddin Auliya was born at Badaun, Amir Khusrau at Patiyali, Sher Shah Suri at Sasaram and Akbar at Umarkot in Sindh, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the birthplace of each figure.

x: Shivaji was born in 1630 at Shivneri Fort near Junnar in Pune district. Umarkot is Akbar's birthplace and Sasaram Sher Shah's.
t: Recall the birthplace of each ruler.

x: All four are correct: Adi Shankaracharya–Kaladi, Ramanujacharya–Sriperumbudur, Basavanna–Bagewadi and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu–Nabadwip.
t: Check each saint's birthplace.

x: The Gupta Era began in 319 AD with Chandragupta I. Saka Samvat (78 AD) goes with Kanishka, the Harsha Era (606 AD) with Harshavardhana, and 1119 AD with Lakshmana Sena.
t: Link each era with its year and ruler.

x: Option C is incorrect: the AD year is the Saka year plus 78, not 77. Saka Samvat began in 78 AD with Kanishka, and Chaitra is its first month.
t: Recall the Saka–AD difference.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Vikrama equals Saka plus 135 (57 BC versus 78 AD), which is exactly why Vikrama Samvat is 135 years ahead.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Vikrama Samvat began in 57/58 BC, the Kali Era in 3102 BC, the Kalachuri/Chedi Era in 248 AD and the Harsha Era in 606 AD, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the starting year of each era.

x: The Lakshmana Sena Era of Bengal began in 1119 AD. 248 AD is the Kalachuri Era, 319 AD the Gupta Era and 606 AD the Harsha Era.
t: Recall the starting year of each era.

x: The Saka Samvat of 78 AD is traditionally credited to the Kushana king Kanishka. Vikramaditya goes with Vikrama Samvat and Chandragupta I with the Gupta Era.
t: Link each era with its ruler.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Krit and Malav Samvat are only other names of the era, not the reason it is linked with victory over the Sakas.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Add 78 to a Saka year to get the AD year: 556 + 78 = 634 AD.
t: Add 78 to the Saka year.

x: Subtract 78 from the AD year to get the Saka year: 2009 − 78 = 1931 Saka.
t: Subtract 78 from the AD year.

x: Add 135 to a Saka year to get the Vikrama year: 465 + 135 = 600, or 601 by the other convention.
t: Add 135 to the Saka year.

x: All three are correct: the Kalachuri/Chedi Era belongs to the Kalachuris, the Gupta Era to Chandragupta I, and the Harsha Era to Harshavardhana.
t: Check each era with its ruler.

x: Vikrama Samvat goes with Vikramaditya, Saka Samvat with Kanishka, the Kalachuri/Chedi Era with the Kalachuris and the Harsha Era with Harshavardhana, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Link each era with its founder.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the Gupta Era of 319 AD marks Chandragupta I's accession, not the founding of the line by Srigupta.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: All four are correct: the Saka calendar, adopted as India's National Calendar in 1957, starts with Chaitra, and Chaitra 1 falls on 22 March, or 21 March in a leap year.
t: Check each fact about the National Calendar.

x: The start of the Kali Era in 3102 BC is traditional, based on legend rather than a historical king. Harsha, the Kalachuris and Kanishka belong to other eras.
t: Discriminate traditional from dynastic eras.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the Harsha Era starts in 606 AD because that is the year Harshavardhana came to the throne.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.
